item.title: Healing as Housekeeping, Not a Makeover
item.description:
Therapy

Healing as Housekeeping, Not a Makeover

Simple, ongoing care makes the biggest difference.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • You don’t need to perform your healing or show up with the “right” words.
  • Therapy is meant to be calm, steady, and focused on helping adults understand what’s happening inside them.
  • Create a space where you can show up as you are, without pressure or judgment.
  • The goal isn’t perfection, it’s feeling more like yourself and building tools that actually fit your life.

Many aspects of therapy culture talk about healing as if it involves some drama or a big reveal, as if there's suddenly a new version of you that has everything figured out. It may sound exciting, but that is not how real change typically works. Most healing is quieter or ordinary. It is the emotional version of housekeeping, such as the small, steady things you do to keep your inner world livable. Housekeeping in therapy isn't flashy, and it doesn't end with applause, but it truly matters. It is also often the part of healing that people overlook because it doesn't feel big enough to "count."

The Real Work Is Small

Makeovers focus on visible results, whereas housekeeping focuses on what actually helps you function.

Healing shows up in simple moments such as:

  • Pausing before reacting
  • Noticing you are overwhelmed sooner than you used to and acting accordingly
  • Saying no without justification
  • Resting before you burn out

These aren't dramatic changes, but they are practical ones. And the ones that last.

Healing Is Maintenance

Source: Ron Lach/Pexels

I am not saying we never think, "If only I could clean my house once and it would stay this way forever," but we know that isn't reasonable. Life creates mess, and things often shift. New needs show up in ways we cannot anticipate. Your emotional life works the same way; you do not just fix something once and never deal with it again. You have to check in with yourself. You adjust. You handle what is in front of you one step at a time. This is not a sign that you aren't doing enough, but instead a sign that you are living.

Clutter Happens

Every home can collect clutter, not because you are doing something wrong, but because you are using the space as intended.

Just like physical clutter in a home, emotional clutter can build up too. This looks like:

  • Stress
  • Old habits
  • Assumptions
  • Judgments
  • Tension
  • Feelings you pushed down

Healing is not about preventing this; it is about noticing when things are piling up and taking time to sit with them before they take over. This might look like a conversation or taking a break, and sometimes it can even be admitting that, hey, I am not OK.

It doesn't always need to be deep to be useful.

Some Things Need Repair

In a home, many things wear down. You have to tighten a screw or patch a wall. It is normal. Just like a home, your internal world needs the same kind of attention. Not everything needs a full renovation. Sometimes it is just repairing one small thing that has been bothering you, such as a belief or a pattern, or a way to talk to yourself.

Small repairs make a big difference.

You Don't Need a New Self

The makeover fantasy says you should become a completely different person. Maybe more confident or more regulated. More everything?

But that is bullsh*t, and healing is not about becoming unrecognizable. It is about making your life easier to live, or it is about creating an internal environment that supports you instead of draining you.

You never need a new self, you just need a cared-for one.

The Work Doesn't End, and That Is Not a Problem

Source: Talena Reese/Pexels

Housekeeping is never-ending; it does not stop. You do not finish it once and declare it done. You maintain it because you want a comfortable living space. Healing is the same. You keep checking in with yourself and keep adjusting. You will keep learning what you need, and that is not a flaw in the process. It is the process.

Remember, healing is not a makeover. It is the ongoing work of taking care of yourself in ways that are simple, steady, and real.

item.title: Why Do Patients Feel Addicted to SSRI/SNRI Antidepressants?
item.description:
SSRIs

Why Do Patients Feel Addicted to SSRI/SNRI Antidepressants?

Antidepressant withdrawal is real—but it isn't an addiction or SUD.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • One in nine U.S. adults took antidepressants in 2023; most (75%) are prescribed by non-psychiatrists.
  • SSRIs and SNRIs aren't addicting—but if stopped, withdrawal symptoms may occur. They may be distressing.
  • Antidepressant withdrawal may feel deeply distressing even when complications are not medically dangerous.

Approximately one in nine American adults takes an antidepressant (AD), the prescriptions written not by psychiatrists but by primary-care clinicians, internists, family physicians, and nurse practitioners. Treatment is often long-term; many patients stay on the medications five years or more.

Depression is far more than ordinary sadness. For many patients, antidepressants are genuinely helpful. Before modern ADs became widely available, severe depression often led to prolonged disability, psychiatric hospitalization, suicide, and greater reliance on electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

Despite the benefits, ADs remain controversial. One of the most common complaints is that patients may say they feel “addicted” because ADs can be difficult to stop. Some patients discontinuing SSRIs or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) ADs say the experience is worse than withdrawing from drugs of abuse. As a result, many conclude that these medications must be addictive. Clinicians generally disagree.

Why Patients May Feel “Addicted”

Let’s say a medication is taken daily for months or years. A dose is missed, and distressing symptoms appear. The medication is restarted, and symptoms improve. The patient concludes, “If I get sick when I stop and better when I restart, I must be addicted.” But difficulty stopping a medication is not the same thing as addiction.

Over time, ADs produce adaptive changes in serotonin- and norepinephrine-related brain circuits. When treatment stops, withdrawal symptoms can occur as the brain readjusts to functioning without those adaptations.

SSRIs and SNRIs can produce what patients call withdrawal symptoms, but they are more accurately called discontinuation symptoms—when stopped abruptly or tapered too quickly.

Many commonly prescribed drugs can produce significant withdrawal or rebound phenomena when stopped abruptly, including corticosteroids, beta-blockers, clonidine, baclofen, and antiepileptics. Some withdrawal syndromes can be medically dangerous and occasionally life-threatening.

Medication Discontinuation Syndromes Occur With Many Medications and also SNRIs and SSRIs
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

ADs belong in this broader category of medications: They may require tapering because physiologic adaptation develops during treatment.

What makes AD withdrawal particularly distressing is that many symptoms are unusual and difficult to describe.

The symptoms may include dizziness, disequilibrium, nausea, flu-like symptoms, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, emotional lability, sensory disturbances, and the so-called “brain zaps” many patients describe as brief electric-shock sensations.

Such experiences can be frightening and may create the impression that something is seriously wrong.

In some cases, symptoms appear within days of stopping treatment or, in extreme cases, missing a pill or two. Certain ADs with shorter half-lives—notably venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, and paroxetine—may produce symptoms after a single missed dose. Patients can develop a powerful association: “If I do not take SSRIs, I immediately become ill.”

That experience feels very similar to addiction, even when the underlying mechanism is different.

Addiction vs. Physical Dependence

The distinction between addiction and physical dependence is central to understanding this discussion.

Addiction is characterized by compulsive use regardless of harm, craving, loss of control, intoxication, and activation of brain reward circuits that reinforce repeated drug-seeking behavior. Addictive substances such as nicotine, heroin and other opioids, cocaine, alcohol, and methamphetamine commonly produce these features.

SSRIs and SNRIs generally do not.

Patients do not take increasing doses of ADs to become intoxicated. They do not seek ADs for euphoria. The medications have no street value, are rarely diverted for recreational use, and do not produce compulsive drug-seeking behavior. ADs do not produce the behavioral features required for diagnosis of a DSM-5 substance use disorder, such as craving, compulsive use, loss of control, or continued use despite harm.

Physical dependence is different. It occurs when the body and brain adjust to the chronic presence of a medication. When the medication is reduced or discontinued, symptoms may emerge as the nervous system readjusts. Physical dependence can and often does occur with many medications not considered addictive.

Cocaine is highly addictive despite lacking the dramatic and medically dangerous withdrawal syndromes seen with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or opioids. Withdrawal symptoms do not define addiction.

Why Antidepressant Withdrawal Can Feel Severe

The intensity of AD discontinuation symptoms cannot be explained simply by the presence of physical symptoms. Withdrawal affects the organ responsible for processing symptoms: the brain.

Many withdrawal syndromes primarily create physiologic discomfort. AD discontinuation may create physiologic symptoms while simultaneously altering mood control, anxiety processing, emotional appraisal, and symptom perception. Patients aren't just experiencing symptoms; they may also become more distressed by those symptoms, more focused on them, and less able to emotionally buffer the experience.

AD discontinuation distress is often described as disproportionately distressing even when it is not typically associated with the medically dangerous complications seen with withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, or certain other drugs.

Another complication is that withdrawal symptoms often resemble the conditions for which ADs were originally prescribed. Patients and clinicians may mistakenly interpret s such symptoms as a relapse of the underlying psychiatric illness rather than as withdrawal. The result is understandable confusion.

Patients may believe they are addicted. Clinicians may believe the illness has returned. But sometimes both interpretations are incorrect.

Not All Antidepressants Carry the Same Risk

Discontinuation risk varies substantially among ADs. Among SSRIs, paroxetine (Paxil) is consistently associated with higher rates of withdrawal symptoms, largely because of its relatively short half-life. Fluoxetine (Prozac) generally carries the lowest discontinuation risk because its long half-life and active metabolite create a built-in tapering effect. Escitalopram (Lexapro) and citalopram (Celexa) fall somewhere in between.

Among newer ADs, some of the highest withdrawal burdens are associated with SNRIs, including venlafaxine (Effexor XR), desvenlafaxine (Pristiq/Khedezla), and duloxetine (Cymbalta).

Duration of treatment also appears important. ADs are frequently taken for years, and longer exposure generally means greater neuroadaptation and potentially greater withdrawal difficulty.

SSRI and SNRI discontinuation symptoms can be uncomfortable and occasionally severe, but are generally less likely to cause life-threatening medical complications than withdrawal from many other commonly prescribed medications, including corticosteroids, antiepileptics, baclofen, clonidine, and beta-blockers.

SSRIs and SNRIs don’t cause addiction, but if stopped, physiologic adaptation to chronic treatment may result in withdrawal symptoms. They’re real and may be distressing

Part of the controversy surrounding ADs may stem from how they have historically been discussed and the resulting patient expectations.

Many patients were told the medications were “non-addictive” and easy to stop. When significant withdrawal symptoms occur, patients may feel misled, dismissed, or even betrayed. The resulting mistrust can be profound.

Most discontinuation symptoms resolve over days to weeks. However, a subset of patients appears to experience more prolonged withdrawal symptoms that may persist for months, although estimates of frequency and risk factors remain uncertain.

Clinicians could improve trust by replacing oversimplified statements with more detailed language. A more accurate explanation might be: SSRIs and SNRIs are not addictive in the traditional sense but can produce physical dependence and clinically meaningful withdrawal symptoms when discontinued, with most cases resulting from abruptly ending or tapering the dose too quickly.

Bottom Line

The brain adapts to long-term AD treatment, and stopping medication abruptly may trigger withdrawal symptoms. That reflects physiologic dependence, not addiction.

AD withdrawal is real, but it is not the same as addiction. Understanding that distinction allows clinicians to remain scientifically accurate while validating patients' experiences. When such conversations are approached with honesty and empathy, patients are better equipped to make informed decisions between pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments, maintain trust in their care, and taper medications safely when the time comes.

item.title: How Social Context Influences Brain Disorders
item.description:
Neuroscience

How Social Context Influences Brain Disorders

A vital new perspective on the interface between brain and culture.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • A new book argues that the link between the brain and mind is “mediated through culture.”
  • Its practical implications extend to rethinking neurodegenerative disease and how we treat it.
  • The neuroplasticity needed to offset and reverse cognitive decline may be found in nutrition and exercise.
Source: Columbia University Press / Used with permission

Matthew Schelke has a gift for metaphors. His preferred one for describing how our brains take on the traits of our culture? “‘Clipping on’ to the social wire.”

Anyone who has hurtled down a zip line knows how thrilling the descent is. “You clip your carabiner onto a thin wire,” Schelke writes in Socially Wired: How Culture Shapes Our Brains, published this week, “then fly through the forest or down from a peak to an unfamiliar destination.”

Especially in old age, though, the clip doesn’t always form a snug fit—it can weaken, grow rusty, and stop working entirely. “When the clip is loosened, as happens in neurological illness,” Schelke notes, “it’s not always a matter of staying on or falling off but often about switching to a different trajectory.”

Challenging the Isolated Brain Model in Neurology

Based on patients seen at Columbia University’s Department of Neurology in New York City, where Schelke was chief resident in 2022-23, Socially Wired begins from the premise that neuroanatomy’s focus on “neural wiring” provides at best an “incomplete metaphor” of the brain in isolation.

Instead—and a challenge to isolationists wedded to the brain’s autonomy—“the link between the brain and mind is mediated through culture.” The dynamism that ensues revolutionizes understanding not just of the brain’s evolving relation to itself, but also of its many “shared affordances”—adopted habits and customs—that act on us psychologically and cerebrally as they pull us into something resembling convergence and adaptation.

“Brain health goes far beyond the skull”

Rendering some brain actions partly cultural, Schelke’s exciting shift in perspective raises a host of medico-philosophical questions for neurological care: “How do our social and cultural worlds transform our brains?” In particular, “What is the nature of the interaction between neural networks and cultural practices?”

Since “as neurologists know, no two patients with the same lesion are alike,” Schelke acknowledges, the case study presents immediate limitations as a genre. Its tendency to dwell on “unique or bizarre individual experiences” is inherently oversimplifying and means it tends to “lack a broader framework.”

Another key theme of Socially Wired is that “manifestations of neurological illness vary widely depending on the social context.” Nevertheless, activities that stimulate the brain—for instance, cooking, singing, dancing, learning new languages and musical instruments, and taking exercise—encourage the neuroplasticity that is needed to offset cognitive decline, in some cases to delay and reverse its damage.

In the case of Gustavo, a sixty-three-year-old high school math teacher in New York City diagnosed with Parkinson’s and prescribed Sinemet (levodopa-carbidopa), he is strongly encouraged to resume his lifelong passion for salsa, and, when dancing is no longer physically possible, to transmute the same energy into administrative work for his club. In Schelke’s formulation, “The music exogenously activates the same basal ganglia networks that are necessary for isochronous gait, facilitating movement and improving ambulation.”

Other chapters tackle crucial contextual questions about strokes—for instance, why an art lover’s glioma in her medial prefrontal cortex leaves her unable to distinguish museum objects she must not touch (but does) from home-made pottery she very much can (and will). Encouraged to teach her granddaughter basic pottery, Laura joins Schelke’s other patients in creating “meaningful forms of intentional action within the framework of their illnesses.”

Practical Implications of Cultural-Mediated Brain Health

With the link between brain and mind firmly “mediated through culture,” an approach involving only on the first will not help us “preserve or improve our mental abilities,” Schelke underscores. Put differently, “the sorts of interventions that are prominent today—medications, supplements, cognitive exercises, dietary changes, neural implants—may be helpful, but they are only half the equation.”

Corroborating the focus of Socially Wired on re-establishing neuroplasticity, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention determined in August 2024 that “nearly 45% of all dementia cases may be prevented or delayed,” and swung its weight behind lifestyle and dietary changes known to aid in the prevention of neurodegenerative disease.

Schelke also aligns silently with the CDC in looking beyond pharmacotherapy, because the drugs prescribed for these conditions are not without controversy. A recent 2026 Cochrane Review on anti-amyloid drugs and their impact, which examined data from 17 clinical trials involving 20,342 participants with mild cognitive impairment, determined: “Drugs that target amyloid beta proteins in the brain likely have no clinically meaningful positive effects, while increasing the risk of bleeding and swelling in the brain. Researchers … found that the absolute effects of anti-amyloid drugs on cognitive decline and dementia severity were absent or trivial.”

Meanwhile, cholinesterase inhibitors like Donepezil, Memantine, and Aricept that are prescribed for chronic dementia are meant to halt the continued breakdown of acetylcholine, a neuro-messenger vital to memory, thinking, and reasoning, yet in some cases have been found to accelerate, not hinder, its destruction. Routine side effects include nausea and appetite suppression, muscle cramps, and difficulty sleeping.

The Role of Diet and Lifestyle in Supporting Brain Health

Above all, if boosting acetylcholine production in the brain is the goal, then a cholinesterase inhibitor may not be necessary. As the website “The Nutrition Source” confirms at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health, “choline is an essential nutrient that is naturally present in certain foods”—walnuts, seeds, berries, legumes, dairy, fish, and poultry—which themselves assist in the removal of amyloid proteins that restrict blood flow in the brain, significantly reducing the risk of stroke and associated cognitive damage.

The neuroplasticity that Schelke wants lifestyle and dietary changes to rescue is not used to peddle false hope about dementia patients’ miraculous recovery from profound cognitive decline. It forms a constructive, evidence-based approach that interrupts the fatalism characterizing decline as inevitable and all else as medically naïve.

Just as the focus on brain health must center lifestyle, exercise, and dietary changes—including foods that boost acetylcholine production without risk of encephalitis and other dangerous adverse effects—so the brain’s complex wiring and capacity to rewire can break open the solipsism of a person and brain experiencing dementia, placing both of them once more in a vast social network where neuronal growth becomes the basis for reducing earlier damage.

item.title: Three Signs that You’re Wise
item.description:
Wisdom

Three Signs that You’re Wise

Rigidity—not stupidity—is the opposite of wisdom.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • Wisdom is the ability to make sound judgments in complex situations that lack clear-cut answers.
  • When faced with complicated problems, wise people identify what they don’t know before declaring what they do.
  • Wisdom recognizes the uniqueness of every situation and avoids the rigid application of universal rules.
  • Wise people consider multiple perspectives, including contrarian viewpoints.

What does it actually mean to be wise? And what does a wise person look like?

As a child, I pictured an old man perched on a mountain, dispensing cryptic one-line advice to pilgrims. But this is such a distorted image of wisdom, not least because it carries a heavy dose of gender bias. And in my own life, some of the wisest people I know are women.

The wise-person-on-a-mountain image also implies that wisdom is about abstract truth and ultimate concerns in life—territory reserved for philosophers and spiritual gurus. But that’s far from the truth. Because we’re conflating intelligence with wisdom.

Smart people generate ideas. Wise people know what to do with them. Aristotle and the Book of Proverbs both point us toward a more grounded understanding: wisdom is practical. It shows up in everyday decisions—like the ones we make at work, with our partners, and in our families. Decisions like how to navigate an intractable conflict between two family members, parent a “difficult” child, or juggle competing deadlines at work.

Psychologist Igor Grossman offers a helpful definition of wisdom–the ability to make sound judgments in complex situations that lack clear-cut answers.

What does that look like in practice? According to Grossman and colleagues, here’re a few signs that you might be displaying more wisdom than you think.

1. You Recognize the Limits of Your Knowledge

This is intellectual humility. Faced with a complicated problem, your first instinct isn’t certainty—it’s curiosity. You notice what you don’t know before declaring what you do.

Instead of rushing to conclusions, you ask questions. You seek counsel. You listen. This might feel counterintuitive. We tend to imagine wise people as advice-givers, not advice-seekers. But throughout the Book of Proverbs, wisdom is consistently linked to seeking guidance. And it makes sense. Overconfidence narrows your perspective; humility expands it.

Here are the kinds of questions wise people tend to ask:

  • What don’t I know that I need to know?
  • Which parts of this situation are knowable—and which aren’t?
  • Who understands this better than I do?
  • Whose perspective can I trust here?

2. You recognize the uniqueness of every situation

Just as overconfidence is an obstacle to wise reasoning, so too is rigidity. In fact, the opposite of wisdom is not stupidity but rigidity. Here’s how rigidity and wisdom differ:

Rigid thinking says: In all situations, do this.

Wise thinking says: In this situation, do this—but in another, do something different.

Ironically, some smart people are prone to rigid thinking. They might think they’ve figured out a framework or a set of values to live by. And then they seek to apply this everywhere.

But reality is messier than any framework. Relentless optimism can be just as unhelpful as constant pessimism. Sometimes you need hope. Sometimes you need caution. Wisdom lies in knowing which is called for—and when. This avoids a one-size-fits-all approach and embraces flexibility, calibration, and adaptability.

If you’re thinking wisely, you might find yourself asking:

  • What unspoken assumptions am I carrying over from a different situation? Should these apply to the current situation?
  • Which past lessons apply here—and which don’t?
  • What’s unique about this moment that’s different from others?
  • Given who’s involved and what I know about them, how should I adjust my response?

3. You Consider Multiple Perspectives

If you’ve ever paused to ask, “What’s the contrarian view on this situation?” you might be practicing wisdom. I used to be frustrated with the types of platitudes floating around online, like:

  • Believe in yourself.
  • Pursue your own dreams—not someone else’s.
  • Be grateful for everything!
  • Never give up.
  • Listen to your own voice; ignore what others think about you.

I now recognize that these aren’t wrong. But they’re incomplete. They represent one viewpoint. But wisdom involves holding—and sometimes integrating—multiple, seemingly conflicting perspectives. Here’re some signs that you’re learning to embrace diverse perspectives:

  • You’re not easily offended by an opposing viewpoint. When someone has a different perspective, your first reaction is curiosity, not judgment.
  • You consult people with a variety of perspectives rather than seek the advice of those who you know will reinforce your original viewpoint.
  • You consider both the short- and long-term consequences of a decision.
  • You have an optimistic vision of the future but also consider what can go wrong.
  • You avoid being a people pleaser, but also reflect on how others might be impacted by your actions.

So…Are You Wise?

If all this sounds familiar, here’s the quiet twist: You might be wiser than you think.

Wise thinking often feels slow. Deliberate. Even uncertain. It can make you envy people who decide quickly and confidently.

But speed isn’t the same as clarity. Your tendency to question assumptions, consult others, and weigh diverse perspectives isn’t a weakness. It’s a strength the world needs more of.

The Individuals In Your Life Who Breed Wisdom and Deserve Gratitude

I’ll conclude with two takeaways:

First, if you’re beginning to recognize your own wisdom, consider where it came from. Who shaped the way you think? Wisdom is rarely self-made. It’s a gift, and the people who contributed to your wisdom deserve your gratitude.

Second, think about the people who have offered you wise counsel. Not the ones who told you exactly what to do, but the ones who asked better questions and invited you to consider multiple perspectives. The ones who inspired you to see more clearly. They didn’t just give you answers. They helped you become someone who can find them. These people truly deserve our thanks.

Wisdom doesn’t live on mountaintops. It lives in the ordinary moments where you pause, deliberate, and choose with care—and in recognizing that you were taught how to do this, often by people who never announced themselves as wise.

This piece is Part 8 of a mini-series on the Varieties of Goodness. It also appears in my Substack newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

item.title: Taking Up Space
item.description:
Social Life

Taking Up Space

Why we need safe, brave, and hope-filled spaces.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • Safe spaces are critical for marginalized populations.
  • The challenge used to be the move from safe to brave spaces.
  • Brave spaces encourage intentional, engaged connections (even if they aren't comfortable).
  • Beyond brave are the spaces we need now—filled with hope and healing.

It’s always been critical to have safe spaces, especially for vulnerable populations. In the 1960s and '70s, the LGBTQA community originated the idea of “safe spaces” to protect people physically and otherwise. These spaces took the form of gay bars, community centers, and support groups—anywhere people could gather without fear of violence for being themselves (Hanhardt, 2020). In the feminist movement, the most empowering spaces were those where women could speak their truths without criticism, fear, or patriarchal constructs (Koch, 2025). It was in these safe spaces that people found not only freedom of expression but also the ability to create community and build solidarity. Classrooms introduced the notion of safe spaces to demonstrate empathy and allyship. bell hooks (2014) urged educators to consider that classrooms were mirrors and extensions of societal constructs that had the power of continued oppression, exploitation, or isolation. Instead, she urged classrooms to be places of freedom.

Physical boundaries where people identified as part of the community through shared symbols like rainbows were clear ways to indicate which spaces were safe. Such symbols are still used today, such as “I am an ally” stickers, social movement buttons, or even campaign-oriented T-shirts. Open language, such as asking someone what pronouns they use, is another way to create psychological safety within physical spaces that extends beyond the classroom. Amy Edmondson (2018), in her definitive work on psychological safety in the workplace, found that it led to a willingness to take interpersonal risks, which in turn led to more innovation and creativity in the organization.

More Than a Safe Space

Safe was a good beginning, but educators like hooks and Freire (1996) felt places of true learning were where people could engage critically and bring their full identities to bear. This was a decisive shift from “safe” spaces to “brave” spaces. Schoolchildren were taught not only to respect diversity but to “stand up” for others. Often, having a brave space required having difficult conversations and processing differences. Journalist Charles Duhigg (2024) identifies the most effective communication as involving “who are we” conversations that are about social identities and being able to be understood, accepted, and contested with respect. Obviously, these are the hardest conversations and require a certain amount of vulnerability and openness, which relates to psychological bravery.

Brave spaces are also characterized by speaking up when silence might be more comfortable, being accountable for mistakes, witnessing human experience, and acknowledging or confronting privilege. The psychological literature assumes that brave spaces are those of intentional, meaningful engagement, but they can also be viewed as environments that have been structured to support courageous actions. Author and facilitator adrienne maree brown (2017) encourages co-creating brave spaces and viewing them through the lens of transformative justice, conflict resolution, and collective accountability. Even though it is difficult, brave spaces continue to be built.

Beyond Brave

With the legislative crackdowns on diversity, equity, and inclusion, and as social norms shift to more politically polarized sentiments, brave spaces are not only rarer but also more exhausting to curate (Ben-Porath, 2023). Add to this the general state of chronic fear and vulnerability that marginalized groups feel, especially in the United States, and brave spaces do not seem to be enough. Further, some activists see brave spaces as an added burden for those who are marginalized (who usually facilitate these spaces) when they already have to navigate everyday structural inequalities.

Hope Lives Here

Where does that leave us? In these times, places of hope are needed. As I have been writing about this year, hope is a protective factor. Indeed, it’s made the difference between surviving socioeconomic and political turmoil and thriving despite the challenges. But how do you fill a space with it?

In a glass and metal building, much like any other office building in Orange County, California, the first thing you might notice is the murals unfurled along the hallways and behind the receptionist desk in old English script declaring, “Hope Lives Here.” This is Project Kinship, an organization that provides support and training to those who have been impacted by incarceration, gangs, and violence, led by Executive Director Steve Kim. Battling challenges of re-entry himself, Steve founded this organization in 1999 and is proud that his staff of over 150 are primarily from system-impacted backgrounds, even on his executive board. Steve shared, “At Kinship, hope became more than just an idea. It became something people could actually feel through belonging, trust, and community. Folks who felt isolated started realizing they weren’t alone anymore. People began showing up for each other in real ways, and that changed everything. That’s when we realized hope wasn’t just something we talked about. It was living in the relationships themselves.”

Hope fills the space physically and metaphorically. For example, it may come into focus in the smell of birria on the stove through the practice of community cooking or the laughter of a group of people in conversation in one of the many seating areas set up in circles instead of the rows that are common in most lobbies. On any given day, there are children playing, students studying, and even a makeshift garden in one of the office cubicles. There can be lively debates, trainings around a whiteboard, and in one corner, two individuals, hands intertwined, offering support to one another. Steve goes on to say, “It’s not easy walking the way of hope. It’s definitely not efficient, but it’s doable, and we just gotta keep doing it.”

Ordinary Magic in Action

You don't need formal spaces to fill with hope. You can do so in simple, easy ways. Try one this week:

  1. Hope rises when power shifts. Try intentionally centering the voices of those with the least systemic power. For instance, ask a child their opinion or to tell you a story from their perspective.
  2. Design for hope. Your interior decor can support hope by being comforting, open, and accessible. Try group seating and more places at the table.
  3. Invite hope in. Space is not always our physical surroundings—invite someone you want to connect with in, ask them how their day was, and then...listen.

item.title: How The 6-6-6 Rule is Affecting Dating
item.description:
Mating

How The 6-6-6 Rule is Affecting Dating

Separating myth and reality in considering a dating mantra.

Posted June 6, 2026

Key points
  • The 6-6-6 rule sets six-feet-tall, six-figure salary, and six-pack abs or six-inch length as minimum limits.
  • It's not clear how many women actually follow the 6-6-6 dating rule. But it is becoming a stereotype of women.
  • Beware of using "women are too picky" as an excuse for dating woes rather than looking at what you are doing.
  • The 6-6-6 rule can be a clear indication of superficiality, which can actually save you time and effort.
The 6-6-6 dating rule is about women only dating men who are at least six feet tall, have at least a six-figure salary, and have six-pack abs or are at least six-inches long down there.
Source: PeopleImages/Getty

You may have heard men on social media complaining about women who want too much "six" when dating. No, not sex, but six with an "I," as in at least some women insisting, "I want a man who is at least six feet tall, has at least a six-figure salary, and has six-pack abs or is at least six-inches long down there." This has become known as the "6-6-6 rule."

Has The 6-6-6 Rule Set Up Unrealistic Dating Expectations for Men?

The men complaining about this rule point to statistics that only 14.5% of men in the U.S. are six feet or taller and only 25% of American men make at least $100,000 a year. It's not clear what percentage of them have six-pack abs or other physical attributes, since such things are more difficult to verify on surveys. But the resulting math suggests that only a very small fraction—likely less than one percent—of all men may satisfy all three or four "sixes."

Are Men Using The 6-6-6 Rule As An Excuse for Dating Problems?

Of course, it's not uncommon for men—and women—to use generalizations about the available dating pool as excuses for their dating woes. The "women are too picky" lament is a common one. Blaming others is often a lot easier than taking a closer look at what you may be doing wrong and then making real constructive changes. And stereotyping entire groups of people can seem a whole lot easier than actually getting to know each individual.

Are Men Using The 6-6-6 Rule to Stereotype Women?

In actuality, it's difficult to tell how many women are in fact using and abiding by the 6-6-6 rule. Sure, some women on social media have been very vocal about ruling out any men who don't meet all "six" criteria of this rule. But how representative are these women?

Regardless, the stereotype is out there. And as is the case with practically any stereotype, you can consciously or unconsciously look for any signs that confirm the stereotype—whether or not they actually do. That can end up tanking dates well before you even have a chance to get to know each other and see if there is a fit.

For example, what if you enter a date thinking your days are already numbered because your salary is short of the six-figure mark? Will you then interpret every statement like "I like traveling" or "I like avocado toast" as "you don't have enough money for me?"

The 6-6-6 Rule Does Show That There are Superficial People Out There

Focusing too heavily on certain superficial characteristics may not get you what you really want.
Source: Alvaro Balderas from Pexels

As is the case with any stereotype, there are indeed some people out there who truly match the stereotype. And women—and men—being superficial is one such case. Plenty of people will rule out others simply based on superficial appearance or thing like salary, overlooking stuff that matters more in the long run such as personal values, goals, and personality.

The Benefits of the 6-6-6 Rule

Now, one benefit of the 6-6-6 rule is that it can be a time- and effort- saver in clearly identifying those who are using more superficial criteria in dating. If someone is clearly all about the sixes and that's just not you, then you could quickly deep-six any possibilities with that person.

The same applies in the opposite direction. If you act all "sixy" because that's how you truly are, that can help other daters more readily choose whether to bother with you. Since dating is about finding the right mutual fit, frank and open communication is key.

Is The 6-6-6 Rule for You?

Therefore, don't waste your time telling others what they should or should not desire. Instead, focus on what you can control: yourself. That then raises the question, if you are looking to date men, should you use the 6-6-6 rule?

Well, you have to ask yourself what kind of six-cess it would end up getting you in the long run? How important are height, salary, abs, and size to you compared to personality, values, and priorities? Sure, six-pack abs may make you more apt to look at the person right now. But over time that six pack may turn into more of a keg. And someone with six or more in length down there may actually be a six or less downer in bed.

Getting someone who is taller or maybe even much taller than you may help if you always want to be looking up or want to minimize use of a step stool. But there's something afoot about setting a six-foot-height limit when so many fawned-over male celebrities don't even top the five-feet-eight-inch mark such as Tom Cruise, Zac Efron, Robert Downey, Jr., and Al Pacino. Finally, setting a somewhat arbitrary salary limit may seem like a way to pay for your future. But you have to ask yourself what you might end up paying for in the process.

Chances are the right fit for you won't necessarily come in the perfect package. Plus, things do change over time. So, maybe it's not a great idea to let too much "six" now get in the way of your dating.
